messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Mariam was 31 when she first came to treatment, a divorced social media manager who had built her life around being quick, polished, and responsive, the kind of person who was always on her phone, always keeping several conversations moving at once. Before the trauma, she had been known among friends and coworkers as calm under pressure. Afterward, she found herself moving through the day with a constant, low-level sense that something terrible might happen at any moment, even in ordinary settings that had once felt entirely safe. She startled badly when someone touched her without warning, her body jolting before she could think, and she often caught herself reacting with the same alarm to harmless sounds or sudden movements at work, as if danger were about to break through the office door. What distressed her most was not only the fear but the intensity of the shame, guilt, and anger that came with it; she described feeling flooded by negative emotions she could not easily settle.

The event she returned to again and again had happened on a crowded evening when she was driving home after work. She had made a split-second mistake behind the wheel and accidentally caused a serious injury to another person. In the aftermath, the scene had lodged in her memory with a force that felt physical. She could sometimes recall the sequence of what happened, but when she tried to describe it to others, she felt words disappear. It was as if she knew the facts and yet could not make them into a coherent story. At other times, she remembered the event in a strangely numb way, as if it had happened to someone else entirely, and that emotional blankness unsettled her almost as much as the vivid moments did. Certain sensory details remained especially potent. She reported that when she thought about the accident, she could sometimes smell the same smells that had been present that night, and those odors seemed to drop her instantly back into the scene, making the memory feel immediate and unavoidable.

In the months that followed, Mariam became increasingly wary of her own judgment. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself to do the right thing, even in situations that had nothing to do with driving. At work, this showed up in small but painful ways. As a social media manager, she was responsible for posting content quickly and making judgment calls in real time, and she began checking and rechecking messages and posts before sending them, worrying that one wrong decision could have irreversible consequences. She described a frightening sense that the person she had become was unrecognizable to her. In the past, she had seen herself as competent and assured; now she felt altered in a way that seemed permanent, as though the accident had changed her for the worse in a manner she could not undo. The divorce, which had already left her life feeling rearranged, also sat heavily in the background of this period, though she did not describe it as the cause of her distress so much as another part of a life that no longer felt familiar.

Her day-to-day environment repeatedly placed her in situations that kept the memory active. In the office, when a colleague brushed past her chair unexpectedly or tapped her shoulder from behind, she recoiled before she could stop herself, embarrassed by how quickly her body moved into alarm. On commutes and in parking lots, she found herself scanning for anything that might go wrong, bracing as though danger could appear without warning. She began avoiding being the first to leave meetings if it meant navigating a busy lot, and she arranged errands to reduce the chances of encountering crowded roads at night. These changes narrowed her world and made her feel increasingly disconnected from the steady, efficient version of herself she had once taken for granted. Even when nothing was wrong, she often felt as if she were waiting for the next disaster.

By the time she sought help, Mariam was exhausted by the ongoing tension between what she knew rationally and what her body seemed to expect. She had reached a point where the startle response, the sudden waves of fear and guilt, and the moments when the memory turned either wordless or eerily numb were interfering with her work and leaving her ashamed in front of others. What finally brought her in was the fear that she would never be able to trust her own judgment again, and that the changed version of herself was permanent. At the same time, she still hoped that treatment might help her feel like herself again, or at least help her make sense of the event without feeling overtaken by it every time a hand landed unexpectedly on her shoulder or a familiar smell brought the night back in full.
